text: Lesson 6's loop finding every Dev-tagged VM and stopping it is genuinely useful logic — useful enough to want in more than one script: a nightly shutdown script, a cost report, an incident-response check. Copy-pasting it into each one works, right up until the tag name changes or a bug shows up, and then it has to be fixed in every copy by hand, with a real risk of quietly missing one of them.

A function gives that logic one name and one home. function Get-StoppedVMs { } names it, following the same Verb-Noun pattern real Az cmdlets use. param() declares what it accepts: [string]$ResourceGroupName, with [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)] meaning PowerShell errors out if it's left off a non-interactive call, rather than silently running with nothing supplied at all.

Once that's defined — loaded into the session, or dot-sourced from its own .ps1 file with a line like . .\AzureHelpers.ps1 — calling it looks exactly like calling a built-in cmdlet: Get-StoppedVMs -ResourceGroupName "rg-prod-web". Nobody calling it needs to see the Get-AzVM and Where-Object logic underneath at all — they just need the name, the one parameter, and what comes back, the same way they'd treat any cmdlet Microsoft shipped as part of the Az module.

A second function can build directly on the first: Start-AllStoppedVMs calls Get-StoppedVMs and loops over whatever it returns, rather than repeating its filtering logic. If the definition of "stopped" ever changes, it changes in exactly one place, and every function built on top picks up the fix automatically — which is also what makes a single function easy to test on its own, apart from the rest of a larger script.

Next: scheduling PowerShell scripts with Azure Automation — running a function like this one on a fixed schedule inside Azure itself, with no laptop that has to stay awake and no VM that has to keep running just to execute it.
